challenges: Mode A, card 1 (practice values): make 100 from 63: 63 + ___ = 100. Answer: 6 needs 3 and 3 needs 6, so 63 + 36 = 99, then add 1: 63 + 37 = 100.

Mode A, card 2 (practice values): make 1,000 from 425: 425 + ___ = 1,000, and 10,000 from 6,284: 6,284 + ___ = 10,000. Answer: 4 needs 5, 2 needs 7 and 5 needs 4, so 425 + 574 = 999, then 425 + 575 = 1,000. The nine partners of 6,284 are 3, 7, 1 and 5, so 6,284 + 3,715 = 9,999, then 6,284 + 3,716 = 10,000.

Mode A, card 3: 'Sukanta likes the numbers 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000. He wants to figure out what number he should add to a given number such that the sum is 100 or 1,000. Help him fill in the blank with an appropriate number. 32 + ___ = 100' and 'Try this method for the number 59. 59 + ___ = 100' Answer: 32 + 68 = 100 and 59 + 41 = 100.

Mode A, card 4: 'Now, use this method to solve the following. 877 + ___ = 1,000 and 666 + ___ = 1,000; 4,103 + ___ = 10,000 and 5,555 + ___ = 10,000.' and 'Will this method work if the units digit is 0? What do you think? What other methods can you use to find the missing number to fill in the blanks? Share your thoughts in the class. (a): 180 + ___ = 1,000; (b): 760 + ___ = 1,000; (c): 400 + ___ = 1,000.' Answer: 877 + 123 = 1,000; 666 + 334 = 1,000; 4,103 + 5,897 = 10,000; 5,555 + 4,445 = 10,000; (a): 820; (b): 240; (c): 600. Yes, the method works with a 0 in the units place, because the last nine is 9 and adding 1 carries. Another way is to count up to the next hundred and then to 1,000. Your words may differ.

Mode B, card 5 (practice values): take away 9 from 84, and take away 99 from 342. Answer: 84: hop back 10 to 74, then forward 1 to 75, so 84 − 9 = 75. 342: hop back 100 to 242, then forward 1 to 243, so 342 − 99 = 243.

Mode B, card 6: 'Namita likes the number 9. She wants to subtract 9 or 99 from any number. Find a way to quickly subtract 9 or 99 from any number. (a): 67 − 9 = ___; (b): 83 − 9 = ___; (c): 144 − 9 = ___; (d): 187 − 99 = ___; (e): 247 − 99 = ___; (f): 763 − 99 = ___.' Answer: (a): 58; (b): 74; (c): 135; (d): 88; (e): 148; (f): 664.

Mode B, card 7: 'Now, use the above solutions to find answers to the following problems. Do not calculate again. Namita wonders if she can get 9 or 99 as the answer to any subtraction problem. Find a way to get the desired answer. (a): 32 − ___ = 9; (b): 56 − ___ = 9; (c): 877 − ___ = 99; (d): 666 − ___ = 99.' Answer: (a): 23; (b): 47; (c): 778; (d): 567.
feedback: Mode A: the digit partner panel lights each pair that makes 9, and the tool says what to do next, for example: 6 and 3 make 9. So 63 + 36 = 99. One more makes 100.

Mode A: a wrong answer shows a soft amber note, for example: 99 is 1 less than 100. Did you add the 1? The tool names the number it expected only after the second try. On a number that ends in 0 the tool says: The method still works. The last nine is 9, and adding 1 carries.
Mode B: each hop writes the result on the line, for example: 84 − 10 = 74, then 74 + 1 = 75. The tool says: 10 is 1 more than 9, so give 1 back. For 99 it says: 100 is 1 more than 99, so give 1 back.

Mode B: a wrong answer shows a soft amber note, for example: You took away 10. Did you give 1 back? For a blank that leaves 9 the tool says: The blank is the first number minus 9: for 47 − ___ = 9, 47 − 10 = 37 and 37 + 1 = 38, so 47 − 38 = 9.
A finished question shows a green tick, the answer in large type and the check, for example 63 + 37 = 100 in Mode A and 84 − 9 = 75 in Mode B.

media.description: Concept video: One video with two labelled sections. Section A shows how to find what to add to reach 100, 1,000 or 10,000 by making 9 in every place and adding 1, and that it always works. Section B shows how to take away 9 or 99 quickly by taking away 10 or 100 and adding 1, and how to use it backwards. It works this example: Part A: Find 46 + ___ = 100 and 358 + ___ = 1,000 by making nines. Part B: Find 52 − 9 and 215 − 99 by taking away 10 or 100 and adding 1 (practice values).
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: you want 46 + ___ = 100. If you first find the number that makes 99, what is it, and what do you do next? Section A: Making 100, 1,000 or 10,000. Make a 9 in every place. In 46, the tens digit 4 needs 5 to make 9 and the ones digit 6 needs 3 to make 9. So 46 + 53 = 99. 99 is 1 less than 100. Add 1 to the number you added: 46 + 54 = 100. The blank is 54. It works for 1,000 too: make 999, then add 1. For 358: 3 needs 6, 5 needs 4 and 8 needs 1, so 358 + 641 = 999, and 358 + 642 = 1,000. It works when the units digit is 0 as well. For 270 the nines are 729, and 270 + 729 = 999, so 270 + 730 = 1,000. You can also count up: 270 + 30 = 300, then 300 + 700 = 1,000. Rule: to find what to add to reach 100, 1,000 or 10,000, make 9 in every place, then add 1. It always works, because 99, 999 and 9,999 are always 1 less than the round number. Section B: Taking away 9 or 99. Predict first: to take 9 away from 52, you can take 10 away first. Did you take away too much or too little, and what do you do about it? 10 is 1 more than 9, so taking 10 away takes 1 too many. Give 1 back: 52 − 10 = 42, then 42 + 1 = 43. So 52 − 9 = 43. 99 is 1 less than 100, so take 100 away and give 1 back. For 215: 215 − 100 = 115, then 115 + 1 = 116. So 215 − 99 = 116. It works backwards too. If 71 − ___ = 9, the blank is 71 − 9 = 62, and you find it with the same trick. Rule: to take away 9, take away 10 and add 1. To take away 99, take away 100 and add 1. To leave 9 or 99, the number to take away is the first number minus 9 or minus 99. 1. Part A. For 46: the tens digit 4 needs 5 to make 9 and the ones digit 6 needs 3 to make 9. So 46 + 53 = 99. 2. 99 is 1 less than 100, so add 1 to the blank: 53 + 1 = 54, and 46 + 54 = 100. 3. For 358: 3 needs 6, 5 needs 4 and 8 needs 1 to make 9. So 358 + 641 = 999. 4. 999 is 1 less than 1,000, so add 1 to the blank: 641 + 1 = 642, and 358 + 642 = 1,000. 5. Part B. 10 is 1 more than 9, so take away 10 and give 1 back. 6. 52 − 10 = 42, and 42 + 1 = 43, so 52 − 9 = 43. 7. 100 is 1 more than 99, so take away 100 and give 1 back. 8. 215 − 100 = 115, and 115 + 1 = 116, so 215 − 99 = 116. 9. Check: 43 + 9 = 52 and 116 + 99 = 215. Answer: Part A: 46 + 54 = 100 and 358 + 642 = 1,000. Part B: 52 − 9 = 43 and 215 − 99 = 116

content.book_number: Quick Sums and Differences: the number 59
content.question: Try this method for the number 59. 59 + ___ = 100
steps: The tens digit 5 needs 4 to make 9, and the ones digit 9 needs 0 to make 9. So 59 + 40 = 99.
Add 1 to the blank: 40 + 1 = 41.
content.answer: The blank is 41, because 59 + 41 = 100.
content.text:
1. The tens digit $5$ needs $4$ to make $9$, and the ones digit $9$ needs $0$ to make $9$. So $59 + 40 = 99$.
2. Add $1$ to the blank: $40 + 1 = 41$.
3. Check: $59 + 41 = 100$.
Answer: The blank is $41$, because $59 + 41 = 100$.

content.book_number: Quick Sums and Differences: 1,000 and 10,000
content.question: Now, use this method to solve the following. 877 + ___ = 1,000 and 666 + ___ = 1,000; 4,103 + ___ = 10,000 and 5,555 + ___ = 10,000.
steps: 877: 8 needs 1, 7 needs 2 and 7 needs 2 to make 9. So 877 + 122 = 999, and the blank is 122 + 1 = 123.
666: each 6 needs 3 to make 9. So 666 + 333 = 999, and the blank is 333 + 1 = 334.
4,103: 4 needs 5, 1 needs 8, 0 needs 9 and 3 needs 6. So 4,103 + 5,896 = 9,999, and the blank is 5,896 + 1 = 5,897.
5,555: each 5 needs 4 to make 9. So 5,555 + 4,444 = 9,999, and the blank is 4,444 + 1 = 4,445.

content.book_number: Quick Sums and Differences: units digit 0
content.question: Will this method work if the units digit is 0? What do you think? What other methods can you use to find the missing number to fill in the blanks? Share your thoughts in the class. (a): 180 + ___ = 1,000; (b): 760 + ___ = 1,000; (c): 400 + ___ = 1,000.
steps: (a): 180: 1 needs 8, 8 needs 1 and 0 needs 9 to make 9. So 180 + 819 = 999, and the blank is 819 + 1 = 820.
(b): 760: 7 needs 2, 6 needs 3 and 0 needs 9. So 760 + 239 = 999, and the blank is 239 + 1 = 240.
(c): 400: 4 needs 5, 0 needs 9 and 0 needs 9. So 400 + 599 = 999, and the blank is 599 + 1 = 600.
Yes, the method works when the units digit is 0. The last nine is 9, and adding 1 makes it carry.
Another method: count up to the next hundred and then to 1,000. For 180: 180 + 20 = 200, then 200 + 800 = 1,000, so the blank is 20 + 800 = 820.
content.answer: Sample answer: (a): 820; (b): 240; (c): 600. Yes, the method works with a 0 in the units place. Your answer may differ.

3. $(c)$: $400$: $4$ needs $5$, $0$ needs $9$ and $0$ needs $9$. So $400 + 599 = 999$, and the blank is $599 + 1 = 600$.

media.description: Question video: Now, use the above solutions to find answers to the following problems. Do not calculate again. Namita wonders if she can get 9 or 99 as the answer to any subtraction problem. Find a way to get the desired answer. (a): 32 − ___ = 9; (b): 56 − ___ = 9; (c): 877 − ___ = 99; (d): 666 − ___ = 99.
media.teaching_notes: 1. The whole is the first number, and the blank and 9 (or 99) are the two parts. So the blank is the first number minus 9 (or minus 99). 2. (a): 32 − 10 = 22, and 22 + 1 = 23. So 32 − 23 = 9. 3. (b): 56 − 10 = 46, and 46 + 1 = 47. So 56 − 47 = 9. 4. (c): The blank is 877 − 99. 877 − 100 = 777, and 777 + 1 = 778. So 877 − 778 = 99. 5. (d): The blank is 666 − 99. 666 − 100 = 566, and 566 + 1 = 567. So 666 − 567 = 99. 6. Check: 32 − 23 = 9, 56 − 47 = 9, 877 − 778 = 99 and 666 − 567 = 99. Answer: (a): 23; (b): 47; (c): 778; (d): 567

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 2,442 a palindrome? Read it from the left, then from the right.
2. From the left it reads 2, 4, 4, 2. From the right it reads 2, 4, 4, 2. It is the same, so 2,442 is a palindrome.
3. 1,231 reads 1, 2, 3, 1 from the left and 1, 3, 2, 1 from the right. It is not the same, so it is not a palindrome.
4. In a palindrome the first digit matches the last digit, and the second digit matches the second from last. The digits do not all have to be the same: 2,442 has two different digits.
5. To list the palindromes between 300 and 340, the first and last digit must be 3 and only the middle digit changes: 303, 313, 323 and 333. 343 is too big.
6. Rule: a palindrome number reads the same both ways. Match the first and last digits, then the next pair in, and so on.

content.text:
Worked example: Is 2,442 a palindrome? List the palindrome numbers between 300 and 340 (practice values).
1. Read 2,442 from the left: 2, 4, 4, 2. Read it from the right: 2, 4, 4, 2. It is the same, so 2,442 is a palindrome.
2. A number between 300 and 340 starts with 3, so it must end with 3. The number is 3, then one digit, then 3.
3. The middle digit can be 0, 1, 2 or 3, because the number must be less than 340. 343 is more than 340.
4. The palindromes are 303, 313, 323 and 333.
5. Check: each of 303, 313, 323 and 333 reads the same from the right.
Answer: 2,442 is a palindrome. Between 300 and 340: 303, 313, 323 and 333

content.question: List all palindrome numbers between 900 and 1,200.
steps: From 900 to 999 the number starts with 9, so it ends with 9. The middle digit is any digit from 0 to 9: 909, 919, 929, 939, 949, 959, 969, 979, 989 and 999.
From 1,000 to 1,200 the number has 4 digits and starts with 1, so it ends with 1. The second digit must match the third digit.
The number is 1, then two digits that match, then 1. With 00 it is 1,001 and with 11 it is 1,111. With 22 it would be 1,221, which is more than 1,200.
Check: 10 numbers below 1,000 and 2 numbers above make 12 palindromes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: in a 2 by 2 grid with the numbers 1 to 4, every row and every column must increase. Which cell must hold 1, and which must hold 4?
2. A row that increases grows to the right. A column that increases grows downwards. So the smallest number must be at the top left, where every row and column starts, and the biggest at the bottom right, where they end.
3. Put 1 at the top left and 4 at the bottom right. Then 2 and 3 go in the other two cells. The top row 1, 2 and the bottom row 3, 4 work.
4. If the rows increase but the columns decrease, a column shrinks downwards. Now 4 must be at the top right and 1 at the bottom left: the top row 3, 4 and the bottom row 1, 2.
5. Check every row and every column, not only the rows.
6. Rule: the arrows tell where the smallest and the biggest number go. Place them, fill the rest, then check every row and every column. Rows are read from left to right and columns from top to bottom.

content.text:
Worked example: Fill a 2 by 2 grid with the numbers 1 to 4 so that every row and column increases. Then fill one so that the rows increase and the columns decrease (practice values).
1. Rows are read left to right and columns top to bottom. An increasing row grows to the right and an increasing column grows downwards.
2. All increasing: the smallest number 1 goes top left and the biggest number 4 goes bottom right.
3. Put 2 and 3 in the other two cells: the top row is 1, 2 and the bottom row is 3, 4.
4. Check the rows: 1 is less than 2 and 3 is less than 4. Check the columns: 1 is less than 3 and 2 is less than 4.
5. Rows increasing and columns decreasing: a column shrinks downwards, so the biggest number 4 goes top right and the smallest number 1 goes bottom left.
6. Put 3 top left and 2 bottom right: the top row is 3, 4 and the bottom row is 1, 2.
7. Check the rows: 3 is less than 4 and 1 is less than 2. Check the columns: 3 is more than 1 and 4 is more than 2.
Answer: Top row 1, 2 and bottom row 3, 4; and top row 3, 4 and bottom row 1, 2

tool_config.idea: Place the numbers 1 to 9 in a 3 by 3 grid so that every row and every column follows its inc or dec arrow, by finding first where the smallest and the biggest number must go.
tool_config.screen: A 3 by 3 floor of tiles in a railway waiting hall, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The grid of nine large square tiles is the largest thing on screen. To the right of each row and under each column sits a small arrow plate with the word inc or dec, as in your maths book. A tray under the grid holds nine number plates, 1 to 9, one of each. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. A rule checker lights the arrow plate of each row and column green when its numbers follow the arrow and soft amber when they break it. Controls: drag a plate into a cell and drag it out again; tap a plate to put it back in the tray; Check; Hint; Undo; Retry (clears the grid); Reset (returns all plates to the tray); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the plates left in the tray, which rows and columns are green or amber, and a card number out of 6. Rows are read left to right and columns top to bottom.
student_does: Look at the small grid from the video with 1 to 4 and every arrow inc. Say where 1 and 4 must go, then press Next.
Fill a small grid whose rows and columns shrink, fill a 3 by 3 grid with the corners given, fill a grid whose rows grow and columns shrink, then repair a grid that has one row breaking its arrow.
The book's own five grids.
challenges: Card 1 (practice values): fill a 2 by 2 grid with 1 to 4 so that every row and column decreases. Answer: 4 goes top left and 1 goes bottom right. For example the top row is 4, 3 and the bottom row is 2, 1.

Card 2 (practice values): the tool puts 1 top left and 9 bottom right. Fill the rest of the 3 by 3 grid so that every row and column increases. Answer: for example 1, 2, 3 over 4, 5, 6 over 7, 8, 9 (many grids work).

Card 3 (practice values): fill a 3 by 3 grid so that every row increases and every column decreases. Answer: the biggest number 9 goes top right and the smallest number 1 goes bottom left. For example 7, 8, 9 over 4, 5, 6 over 1, 2, 3.

Card 4 (practice values): the grid shows 1, 2, 3 over 4, 6, 5 over 7, 8, 9 with every arrow inc, and the middle row is amber. Swap two plates to repair it. Answer: swap the 6 and the 5, so the middle row is 4, 5, 6.

Each number should be used only once.' and 'This time, fill the grid such that each row and column has numbers in decreasing (dec) order.' Answer: for example 1, 2, 3 over 4, 5, 6 over 7, 8, 9 for inc, and 9, 8, 7 over 6, 5, 4 over 3, 2, 1 for dec. Your grids may differ.

Grid 2: rows dec, dec, inc and columns dec, dec, inc. Grid 3: rows inc, inc, dec and columns inc, dec, dec. A plate placed where it cannot work is never refused: the row and column turn soft amber and stay that way until they follow their arrows.

A finished grid shows every arrow plate green, a tick and the grid read out as three rows.

media.description: Concept video: Show how the inc and dec arrows tell where the smallest and the biggest number go in a grid, and how to fill and check a grid, as a warm-up for the grid puzzle. It works this example: Fill a 2 by 2 grid with the numbers 1 to 4 so that every row and column increases. Then fill one so that the rows increase and the columns decrease (practice values).
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: in a 2 by 2 grid with the numbers 1 to 4, every row and every column must increase. Which cell must hold 1, and which must hold 4? A row that increases grows to the right. A column that increases grows downwards. So the smallest number must be at the top left, where every row and column starts, and the biggest at the bottom right, where they end. Put 1 at the top left and 4 at the bottom right. Then 2 and 3 go in the other two cells. The top row 1, 2 and the bottom row 3, 4 work. If the rows increase but the columns decrease, a column shrinks downwards. Now 4 must be at the top right and 1 at the bottom left: the top row 3, 4 and the bottom row 1, 2. Check every row and every column, not only the rows. Rule: the arrows tell where the smallest and the biggest number go. Place them, fill the rest, then check every row and every column. Rows are read from left to right and columns from top to bottom. 1. Rows are read left to right and columns top to bottom. An increasing row grows to the right and an increasing column grows downwards. 2. All increasing: the smallest number 1 goes top left and the biggest number 4 goes bottom right. 3. Put 2 and 3 in the other two cells: the top row is 1, 2 and the bottom row is 3, 4. 4. Check the rows: 1 is less than 2 and 3 is less than 4. Check the columns: 1 is less than 3 and 2 is less than 4. 5. Rows increasing and columns decreasing: a column shrinks downwards, so the biggest number 4 goes top right and the smallest number 1 goes bottom left. 6. Put 3 top left and 2 bottom right: the top row is 3, 4 and the bottom row is 1, 2. 7. Check the rows: 3 is less than 4 and 1 is less than 2. Check the columns: 3 is more than 1 and 4 is more than 2. Answer: Top row 1, 2 and bottom row 3, 4; and top row 3, 4 and bottom row 1, 2
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

Check the rows: each one grows to the right. Check the columns: 1, 4, 7 and 2, 5, 8 and 3, 6, 9 each grow downwards.

modules.module_summary: Even and odd numbers and their sums, two thinking puzzles about coins and a torch, reading tables, and a revision of the whole road trip.

segments.summary: A number is even when its counters pair up with none left, and odd when one is left. The units digit tells: 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 are even.

topic_objective.objective_text: Students decide whether a number is even or odd by pairing counters and by looking at the units digit.

content.text:
1. Predict first: you put 14 counters in pairs, then 15 counters in pairs. Which one has a counter left over?
2. 14 counters make 7 pairs and none is left over. A number is even when its counters pair up with none left.
3. 15 counters make 7 pairs and 1 counter is left over. A number is odd when one counter is left over.
4. You do not need to draw counters for big numbers. Look at the units digit. If it is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 the number is even. If it is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 it is odd.
5. 3,468 ends in 8, so it is even. 5,127 ends in 7, so it is odd. 0 counts as even, so a number that ends in 0 is even.
6. Rule: even means pairs with none left, odd means one left over. The units digit tells which.

content.text:
Worked example: Arrange 14 counters and 15 counters in pairs. Then say whether 3,468 and 5,127 are even or odd (practice values).
1. 14 counters make 7 pairs: 7 + 7 = 14, and no counter is left over. So 14 is even.
2. 15 counters make 7 pairs and 1 counter is left over: 7 + 7 + 1 = 15. So 15 is odd.
3. For big numbers look at the units digit: 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 mean even, and 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 mean odd.
4. 3,468 has the units digit 8, so it is even.
5. 5,127 has the units digit 7, so it is odd.
6. Check: 3,468 = 1,734 + 1,734, two equal parts, so nothing is left over.
Answer: 14 and 3,468 are even; 15 and 5,127 are odd

media.context: We the Travellers - II. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: Show that an even number pairs up with none left over and an odd number has one left over, and that the units digit tells which. It works this example: Arrange 14 counters and 15 counters in pairs. Then say whether 3,468 and 5,127 are even or odd (practice values).
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: you put 14 counters in pairs, then 15 counters in pairs. Which one has a counter left over? 14 counters make 7 pairs and none is left over. A number is even when its counters pair up with none left. 15 counters make 7 pairs and 1 counter is left over. A number is odd when one counter is left over. You do not need to draw counters for big numbers. Look at the units digit. If it is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 the number is even. If it is 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 it is odd. 3,468 ends in 8, so it is even. 5,127 ends in 7, so it is odd. 0 counts as even, so a number that ends in 0 is even. Rule: even means pairs with none left, odd means one left over. The units digit tells which. 1. 14 counters make 7 pairs: 7 + 7 = 14, and no counter is left over. So 14 is even. 2. 15 counters make 7 pairs and 1 counter is left over: 7 + 7 + 1 = 15. So 15 is odd. 3. For big numbers look at the units digit: 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 mean even, and 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 mean odd. 4. 3,468 has the units digit 8, so it is even. 5. 5,127 has the units digit 7, so it is odd. 6. Check: 3,468 = 1,734 + 1,734, two equal parts, so nothing is left over. Answer: 14 and 3,468 are even; 15 and 5,127 are odd

content.text:
1. Predict first: you join 9 counters and 13 counters. Each group has 1 counter left over. What happens to the two leftover counters?
2. The two leftover counters make one new pair, so nothing is left over. 9 + 13 = 22 is even.
3. Even plus even: neither group has a leftover, so the joined group has none. 14 + 8 = 22 is even.
4. Odd plus even: only one group has a leftover and it stays alone. 7 + 10 = 17 is odd.
5. Rule: even plus even is even, odd plus odd is even, odd plus even is odd. It is true for every pair, because the leftovers decide.

content.text:
Worked example: Join 14 and 8, then 9 and 13, then 7 and 10, and say whether each sum is even or odd (practice values).
1. 14 and 8 are both even, so no counter is left over in either group: 14 + 8 = 22, and 22 is even.
2. 9 and 13 are both odd, so each group has 1 counter left over. The two leftovers make one pair: 9 + 13 = 22, and 22 is even.
3. 7 is odd and 10 is even, so only 7 has a leftover counter. It stays alone: 7 + 10 = 17, and 17 is odd.
4. Check: 22, 22 and 17 end in 2, 2 and 7, so they are even, even and odd.
Answer: 14 + 8 = 22 is even; 9 + 13 = 22 is even; 7 + 10 = 17 is odd

9 and 13 are both odd, so each group has 1 counter left over. The two leftovers make one pair: 9 + 13 = 22, and 22 is even.
7 is odd and 10 is even, so only 7 has a leftover counter. It stays alone: 7 + 10 = 17, and 17 is odd.
Check: 22, 22 and 17 end in 2, 2 and 7, so they are even, even and odd.
content.answer: 14 + 8 = 22 is even; 9 + 13 = 22 is even; 7 + 10 = 17 is odd

tool_config.title: Pairs and Leftovers
tool_config.idea: Arrange draggable counters into pairs, in two clearly separated activities. Activity 1, Pair up: decide whether a number is even or odd by pairing counters, with any leftover counter made visible. Activity 2, Combine two groups: join two counter groups, pair the joined group and inspect the leftover to see what happens in the sum of two even numbers, two odd numbers, and an odd and an even number. Activity 2 opens after Activity 1 is done.
tool_config.screen: A wooden board on a bench at a bus stand with round blue counters, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. Two big activity tabs sit at the top, Activity 1: Pair up and Activity 2: Combine two groups, and only one activity is on screen at a time. In Activity 1 the board shows one large drop zone for a group of counters. In Activity 2 it shows a drop zone for Group 1, one for Group 2 and a combine zone between them. The counters in the zones are the largest things on screen. A counter group is arranged in two rows so that each counter in the top row is paired with the one below it; a counter with no partner is marked with a small orange ring. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it, and it is the activity's own sentence. Beside each group is its number in large type and an even or odd tag that appears after the student answers. Controls in Activity 1: a stepper for the number of counters (0 to 40); drag counters in or out; tap Pair up to arrange the group in two rows; answer cards even and odd. Controls in Activity 2: a stepper for the number of counters in each group; tap Pair up to arrange a group in two rows; tap Combine to join Group 1 and Group 2 in the combine zone, then tap Pair up again to pair the joined group; answer cards even and odd for the sum; for the book's questions a Choose a pair button that stores each chosen pair and its sum. In both: Check; Hint; Retry (clears this card); Reset (restores the board); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number in each group, the number of pairs, the number of leftover counters (0 or 1), the joined number, and a card number out of 7.

Activity 2: look at the board from the video with 9 counters and 13 counters, each with a ringed leftover. Say what the two leftovers make when the groups join, then press Next.
Activity 1: pair up groups of counters and tag each one even or odd. Activity 2: combine two even groups, two odd groups, and an odd and an even group, pair the joined group and read its leftover.
Activity 2: the book's three questions, five pairs of two even numbers, five pairs of two odd numbers and five pairs of an odd and an even number, with what you notice about their sums.
challenges: Activity 1, card 1 (practice values): pair up 16 counters, then 21 counters, then 30 counters, and tag each one. Answer: 16 makes 8 pairs with none left over, so it is even. 21 makes 10 pairs with 1 left over, so it is odd. 30 makes 15 pairs with none left over, so it is even, like every number that ends in 0.

Activity 2, card 2 (practice values): combine Group 1 with 6 counters and Group 2 with 10 counters, and pair the joined group. Answer: 6 + 10 = 16, no leftover in either group, so the joined group has none and 16 is even.

Activity 2, card 3 (practice values): combine Group 1 with 11 counters and Group 2 with 15 counters. Answer: each group has 1 leftover. The two leftovers make one pair, so 11 + 15 = 26 has none left over and is even.

Activity 2, card 4 (practice values): combine Group 1 with 19 counters and Group 2 with 6 counters. Answer: only the group of 19 has a leftover, and it stays alone, so 19 + 6 = 25 has 1 left over and is odd.

Activity 2, card 5: 'What do you notice about the sums in each of the following cases? Do you think it will be true for all pairs of such numbers? Explain your observations. You may use the paired arrangement to explain your thinking. (a): 12 and 6 are a pair of even numbers. Choose 5 such pairs of even numbers. Add the numbers in each of the pairs.' Sample answer: 12 + 6 = 18, 4 + 8 = 12, 10 + 20 = 30, 14 + 16 = 30 and 2 + 6 = 8. Every sum is even, for all such pairs, because two even numbers pair up with none left over. Your pairs may differ.

Activity 2, card 6: 'What do you notice about the sums in each of the following cases? Do you think it will be true for all pairs of such numbers? Explain your observations. You may use the paired arrangement to explain your thinking. (b): 13 and 9 are a pair of odd numbers. Choose 5 such pairs of odd numbers. Add the numbers in each of the pairs.' Sample answer: 13 + 9 = 22, 3 + 5 = 8, 7 + 11 = 18, 15 + 1 = 16 and 9 + 9 = 18. Every sum is even, for all such pairs, because each odd number has 1 left over and the two leftovers make a pair. Your pairs may differ.

Activity 2, card 7: 'What do you notice about the sums in each of the following cases? Do you think it will be true for all pairs of such numbers? Explain your observations. You may use the paired arrangement to explain your thinking. (c): 7 and 12 are a pair of odd and even numbers. Choose 5 such pairs of odd and even numbers. Add the numbers in each of the pairs.' Sample answer: 7 + 12 = 19, 3 + 4 = 7, 5 + 10 = 15, 9 + 2 = 11 and 11 + 8 = 19. Every sum is odd, for all such pairs, because the odd number's leftover has no partner. Your pairs may differ.

concepts.concept_name: Paying an Exact Amount with Coins

content.text:
1. Predict first: a purse has 2 coins of ₹5, 3 coins of ₹2 and 4 coins of ₹1. Is there only one way to pay ₹12, or more than one?
2. Go through the coins one kind at a time, starting with the ₹5 coins. Try 2 coins of ₹5, then 1 coin, then none.
3. With 2 coins of ₹5, which make ₹10, ₹2 more is needed: 1 coin of ₹2, or 2 coins of ₹1. That is 2 ways.
4. With 1 coin of ₹5, ₹7 more is needed: 3 coins of ₹2 and 1 coin of ₹1, or 2 coins of ₹2 and 3 coins of ₹1. That is 2 more ways.
5. With no ₹5 coin, all the ₹2 and ₹1 coins make only ₹10, which is not enough. So there are 4 ways in all.
6. Rule: take the coins of the biggest kind first, try each number of them, and fill the rest with smaller coins. Keep a list so no way is missed.

content.text:
Worked example: A purse has 2 coins of ₹5, 3 coins of ₹2 and 4 coins of ₹1. List all the ways to pay ₹12 exactly (practice values).
1. Try the ₹5 coins first: 2 coins, 1 coin or none.
2. 2 coins of ₹5 make ₹10, and ₹2 more is needed. Use 1 coin of ₹2, or 2 coins of ₹1: 10 + 2 = 12.
3. 1 coin of ₹5 makes ₹5, and ₹7 more is needed. Use 3 coins of ₹2 and 1 coin of ₹1: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12. Or use 2 coins of ₹2 and 3 coins of ₹1: 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.
4. With no ₹5 coin, all the ₹2 and ₹1 coins make 6 + 4 = 10 rupees, which is not enough for ₹12.
5. So there are 4 ways in all: 5 + 5 + 2, 5 + 5 + 1 + 1, 5 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 and 5 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1.
6. Check: 5 + 5 + 2 = 12 and 5 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 12.
Answer: 4 ways, for example 5 + 5 + 2 = 12 and 5 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 12

content.book_number: Let Us Think: Jincy's coins
content.question: Jincy opened her piggy bank. She found 8 coins of ₹1, 9 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹5. She wants to buy stickers worth ₹38. What possible combination of coins can she use to pay the exact amount?
steps: All the coins together make 8 + 18 + 25 = 51 rupees: 8 coins of ₹1 make ₹8, 9 coins of ₹2 make ₹18 and 5 coins of ₹5 make ₹25. So ₹38 can be paid.
Go through the number of ₹5 coins, from the most (5) to the fewest, and fill the rest with ₹2 and ₹1 coins.

5 coins of ₹5 make ₹25, and ₹13 more is needed: 6 coins of ₹2 and 1 coin of ₹1, or 5 coins of ₹2 and 3 coins of ₹1, or 4 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹1, or 3 coins of ₹2 and 7 coins of ₹1. That is 4 ways.

4 coins of ₹5 make ₹20, and ₹18 more is needed: 9 coins of ₹2, or 8 coins of ₹2 and 2 coins of ₹1, or 7 coins of ₹2 and 4 coins of ₹1, or 6 coins of ₹2 and 6 coins of ₹1, or 5 coins of ₹2 and 8 coins of ₹1. That is 5 ways.
3 coins of ₹5 make ₹15, and ₹23 more is needed: 9 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹1, or 8 coins of ₹2 and 7 coins of ₹1. That is 2 ways.
With 2 coins of ₹5, which make ₹10, ₹28 more is needed, but all the ₹2 and ₹1 coins make only 18 + 8 = 26 rupees. So it cannot be done, and fewer ₹5 coins is even less possible.
In all there are 4 + 5 + 2 = 11 combinations.
Check one: 5 coins of ₹5, 6 coins of ₹2 and 1 coin of ₹1 make 25 + 12 + 1 = 38.
content.answer: Sample answer: 5 coins of ₹5, 6 coins of ₹2 and 1 coin of ₹1 make 25 + 12 + 1 = 38. There are 11 combinations in all. Your answer may differ.

concepts.concept_name: ON and OFF, Press by Press

content.text:
1. Predict first: a torch is OFF. You press its switch 14 times. Is the torch ON or OFF after the 14th press?
2. Press 1 turns it ON, press 2 turns it OFF, press 3 turns it ON, press 4 turns it OFF. The torch keeps taking turns.
3. ON comes after the odd presses 1, 3, 5, 7 and so on. OFF comes after the even presses 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on.
4. You do not have to press 14 times. 14 is even, so the torch is OFF. For the 31st press, 31 is odd, so the torch is ON.
5. Rule: a switch that flips with every press is ON after an odd press and OFF after an even press. Look at whether the press number is odd or even.

content.text:
Worked example: A torch is OFF at the start and each press of its switch flips it. Is the torch ON or OFF after the 14th press and after the 31st press? Which presses give ON? (practice values)
1. Press 1 gives ON, press 2 gives OFF, press 3 gives ON. The torch takes turns.
2. The odd presses 1, 3, 5, and so on give ON. The even presses 2, 4, 6, and so on give OFF.
3. 14 is even because it ends in 4, so after the 14th press the torch is OFF.
4. 31 is odd because it ends in 1, so after the 31st press the torch is ON.
5. Check: every 2 presses bring the torch back to OFF, and 14 = 7 + 7 is 7 pairs of presses, so the torch is OFF.
Answer: OFF after the 14th press and ON after the 31st press; ON after odd presses, OFF after even presses

content.book_number: Let Us Think: Raghu's torch, the 23rd press
content.question: Raghu is fond of his grandfather's torch. He starts playing with it. He presses the switch once and the light turns ON. He presses it a second time and the light turns OFF. content.text:
1. Predict first: a table lists three buses with the kilometres they travelled: 4,215, 6,380 and 5,094. How do you find which bus travelled the most, and how much more than the least?
2. Section A: Reading a table.
3. A table has rows and columns. Each row is one thing, here one bus, and each column is one fact about it, such as the distance or the year.
4. To find the highest, compare the numbers in a column. 6,380 is more than 5,094 and 4,215, so Bus B travelled the most. The lowest is 4,215, Bus A.
5. To find the difference between two values, subtract the smaller from the bigger: 6,380 − 4,215 = 2,165.
6. To find a birth year from an age, take the age from the year. If a driver was 25 in 2021, the driver was born in 2021 − 25 = 1996.
7. Rule: read the row and the column, compare to find the highest and the lowest, and subtract the smaller from the bigger to find a difference.
8. Section B: Enough, short or extra?
9. Predict first: 12,450 tickets were printed and 12,615 people came. Were there enough tickets?
10. Compare the two numbers. 12,615 is more than 12,450, so more people came than tickets were printed. The tickets were not enough.
11. How many were short? Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 12,615 − 12,450 = 165. So 165 tickets were short.
12. On another day 9,830 tickets were printed and 9,415 people came. The tickets are more than the people, so they are enough. The extra tickets are 9,830 − 9,415 = 415.
13. Rule: compare what was printed with what was needed. If the printed number is less, the difference is how many are short. If it is more, the difference is how many are extra.

content.text:
Worked example: Part A: A table shows three buses. Bus A travelled 4,215 km and was bought in 2015, Bus B travelled 6,380 km and was bought in 2018, and Bus C travelled 5,094 km and was bought in 2021. Which bus travelled the most? What is the difference between the most and the least, and between Bus B and Bus C? A driver was 25 years old when Bus C was bought. In which year was the driver born? Part B: 12,450 tickets were printed for a fair and 12,615 people came. Were the tickets enough, and how many were short or extra? On another day 9,830 tickets were printed and 9,415 people came (practice values).
1. Part A. Compare the distances: 6,380 is the most, so Bus B travelled the most. 4,215 is the least, so Bus A travelled the least.
2. The difference between the most and the least is 6,380 − 4,215 = 2,165 km.
3. The difference between Bus B and Bus C is 6,380 − 5,094 = 1,286 km.
4. Bus C was bought in 2021 and the driver was 25 then, so the driver was born in 2021 − 25 = 1996.
5. Check: 4,215 + 2,165 = 6,380, 5,094 + 1,286 = 6,380 and 1996 + 25 = 2021.
6. Part B. Compare 12,450 and 12,615. 12,450 is less than 12,615, so the tickets were not enough.
7. The number short is 12,615 − 12,450 = 165.
8. Compare 9,830 and 9,415. 9,830 is more than 9,415, so the tickets were enough.
9. The number extra is 9,830 − 9,415 = 415.
10. Check: 12,450 + 165 = 12,615 and 9,415 + 415 = 9,830.
Answer: Part A: Bus B travelled the most; 2,165 km; 1,286 km; the driver was born in 1996. Part B: first day: not enough, 165 short; second day: enough, 415 extra

tool_config.screen: A travel information board in a station hall on the road trip, drawn as a warm 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The board is a large table with a heading at the top of every column and its unit beside it, for example km or year, and one row for each thing; the table is the largest thing on screen and its numbers are in large type. The book's own tables are shown as the book prints them, with the same rows, the same headings and the same numbers. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. A compare strip under the board shows two chosen numbers with the bigger first, the minus sign and a blank for the difference. Controls: tap a row to light it and tap a column heading to light the column, and the cell where they meet glows orange; tap two numbers of one column to put them in the compare strip; type the difference in the blank; for a printed number against a number of people, answer cards Sufficient, Short and Extra and a box for how many; type a year or a name in an answer box; Check; Hint; Undo; Retry (clears the answers of this card); Reset (restores the board); Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the row and column in focus, the two numbers compared, the difference, and a card number out of 6.

challenges: Card 1 (practice values): a railway board shows Train A 2,865 km and 2009, Train B 1,978 km and 2014, Train C 3,412 km and 2011, Train D 2,149 km and 2018, with the headings Distance in km and Year started. What unit is the distance column in, and how far does Train C run? Answer: kilometres, and Train C runs 3,412 km.

Card 2 (practice values): on the same board, which train runs the longest distance, how much longer is it than the shortest, and what is the difference between Train A and Train D? media.title: Reading a Table: Highest, Difference, Short or Extra
media.context: We the Travellers - II. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Concept video: One video with two labelled sections. Section A shows how to read a table to find the highest and lowest values, the difference between two values and a year from an age. Section B shows how to compare the number printed with the number needed and decide whether it is enough, short or extra, and by how many. It works this example: Part A: A table shows three buses. Bus A travelled 4,215 km and was bought in 2015, Bus B travelled 6,380 km and was bought in 2018, and Bus C travelled 5,094 km and was bought in 2021. Which bus travelled the most? What is the difference between the most and the least, and between Bus B and Bus C? A driver was 25 years old when Bus C was bought. In which year was the driver born? Part B: 12,450 tickets were printed for a fair and 12,615 people came. Were the tickets enough, and how many were short or extra? On another day 9,830 tickets were printed and 9,415 people came (practice values).
media.teaching_notes: Predict first: a table lists three buses with the kilometres they travelled: 4,215, 6,380 and 5,094. How do you find which bus travelled the most, and how much more than the least? Section A: Reading a table. A table has rows and columns. Each row is one thing, here one bus, and each column is one fact about it, such as the distance or the year. To find the highest, compare the numbers in a column. 6,380 is more than 5,094 and 4,215, so Bus B travelled the most. The lowest is 4,215, Bus A. To find the difference between two values, subtract the smaller from the bigger: 6,380 − 4,215 = 2,165. To find a birth year from an age, take the age from the year. If a driver was 25 in 2021, the driver was born in 2021 − 25 = 1996. Rule: read the row and the column, compare to find the highest and the lowest, and subtract the smaller from the bigger to find a difference. Section B: Enough, short or extra? Predict first: 12,450 tickets were printed and 12,615 people came. Were there enough tickets? Compare the two numbers. 12,615 is more than 12,450, so more people came than tickets were printed. The tickets were not enough. How many were short? Subtract the smaller from the bigger: 12,615 − 12,450 = 165. So 165 tickets were short. On another day 9,830 tickets were printed and 9,415 people came. The tickets are more than the people, so they are enough. The extra tickets are 9,830 − 9,415 = 415. Rule: compare what was printed with what was needed. If the printed number is less, the difference is how many are short. If it is more, the difference is how many are extra. 1. Part A. Compare the distances: 6,380 is the most, so Bus B travelled the most. 4,215 is the least, so Bus A travelled the least. 2. The difference between the most and the least is 6,380 − 4,215 = 2,165 km. 3. The difference between Bus B and Bus C is 6,380 − 5,094 = 1,286 km. 4. Bus C was bought in 2021 and the driver was 25 then, so the driver was born in 2021 − 25 = 1996. 5. Check: 4,215 + 2,165 = 6,380, 5,094 + 1,286 = 6,380 and 1996 + 25 = 2021. 6. Part B. Compare 12,450 and 12,615. 12,450 is less than 12,615, so the tickets were not enough. 7. The number short is 12,615 − 12,450 = 165. 8. Compare 9,830 and 9,415. 9,830 is more than 9,415, so the tickets were enough. 9. The number extra is 9,830 − 9,415 = 415. 10. Check: 12,450 + 165 = 12,615 and 9,415 + 415 = 9,830. Answer: Part A: Bus B travelled the most; 2,165 km; 1,286 km; the driver was born in 1996. Part B: first day: not enough, 165 short; second day: enough, 415 extra

content.text:
1. Predict first: you have driven the whole road trip, from the number cards to the tables. Can you say one idea from each stop? Read the lines below and tick each idea you remembered.
2. Swapping: when a smaller number and a bigger number change groups, one sum goes up and the other goes down by the same amount. To make two sums equal, swap two numbers whose difference is half of the gap.
3. Check: the groups 2, 6, 9 and 4, 7, 10 add up to 17 and 21. Swap 2 and 4 and both groups add up to 19.
4. Adding: add one place at a time from the ones, and regroup 10 as 1 of the next place. For 67 + 58: 7 + 8 = 15, then 6 + 5 + 1 = 12, so the sum is 125.
5. Easier ways: a number just below a round number can be added by adding the round number and taking the extra back. 54 + 98 = 54 + 100 − 2 = 152.
6. Subtracting and the link: regroup 1 ten as 10 ones when there are too few ones, and check by adding. 72 − 38 = 34 and 38 + 34 = 72. From 35 + 28 = 63 you also know 63 − 28 = 35.
7. Consecutive numbers: the difference between successive sums is the number of numbers added, and pairs from the two ends make the same total. 41 + 42 + 43 + 44 + 45 = 5 × 43 = 215.
8. Large numbers: the same steps as small numbers, with the digits aligned. 3,486 + 2,729 = 6,215 and 6,402 − 2,758 = 3,644.
9. Journey problems: read one step at a time, add for gets and totals, take away for spends and what is left, and estimate first by rounding up. 15,000 − 4,250 + 2,000 − 3,160 = 9,590.
10. Round numbers: make nines and add 1 to reach 100, and take away 10 or 100 then add 1 to take away 9 or 99. 46 + 54 = 100 and 52 − 9 = 43.
11. Palindromes: a palindrome number reads the same both ways. 2,442 is one, and the palindromes from 300 to 340 are 303, 313, 323 and 333.
12. Grids: the arrows tell where the smallest and the biggest number go. Check every row and every column.
13. Even and odd: pairs with none left over mean even, and one left over means odd. Even plus even is even, odd plus odd is even and odd plus even is odd.
14. Coins and the switch: list the ways one kind of coin at a time. A switch that flips with each press is ON after an odd press and OFF after an even press.
15. Tables: subtract the smaller from the bigger to find a difference. 6,380 − 4,215 = 2,165. If the number printed is less than the number needed, the difference is how many are short.
16. Check: is 17 + 6 odd or even? 17 + 6 = 23, which is odd, because 17 is odd and 6 is even.
17. Check: find 87 + ___ = 100. 87 needs 12 to make 99, so the blank is 13.
18. Check: add 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 by pairs. 6 + 9 = 15 and 7 + 8 = 15, so the sum is 15 + 15 = 30.

objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students explain with leftover counters why even plus even is even, odd plus odd is even, and odd plus even is odd.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students use the leftover counters to explain the sums of two even numbers, two odd numbers, and an odd and an even number.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students list all the ways to pay an exact amount with a limited number of coins by taking the coins of the biggest kind first.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students list the coin combinations that pay an exact amount by going through the coins of the biggest kind one at a time.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students tell whether a switch is on or off after a given press by deciding if the press number is odd or even.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students tell whether a torch is on or off after any press by deciding whether the press number is odd or even.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students read a table to find the highest and lowest values and the difference between two values, and decide whether a number is enough, short or extra.
objectives.strand_name: Even and Odd, Thinking Puzzles and Tables

objectives.objective_text: Students read the mountain table and the certificate table to find the highest and lowest values, the differences, and how many are short or extra.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (a): Group 1: 1, 2, 7, 9 (sum 19). Group 2: 3, 4, 5, 9 (sum 21).

Book item: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (b): Group 1: 5, 7, 12, 15 (sum 39). Group 2: 9, 11, 13, 14 (sum 47).

Book item: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (c): Group 1: 11, 15, 19, 23 (sum 68). Group 2: 13, 17, 21, 25 (sum 76).

Book item: In each of the following, there are two groups of numbers. Look carefully at the numbers in each group and their sums. Interchange pairs of numbers between the two groups to make their sums equal. Try to do this using the least number of moves. (d): Group 1: 77, 78, 79, 80 (sum 314). Group 2: 81, 82, 83, 84 (sum 330).
Book item: A lorry has 28 litres of fuel in its tank. An additional 75 litres is filled. What is the total quantity of fuel in the lorry?
Book item: Let us try one more. Find the sum of 49 and 89.
Book item: Add the following numbers. Wherever possible, find easier ways to add the pairs of numbers. (a): 15 + 79; (b): 46 + 99; (c): 38 + 35; (d): 5 + 89; (e): 76 + 28; (f): 69 + 20.

Book item: Find the relationship between the numbers in the given statements and fill in the blanks appropriately. (a): If 46 + 21 = 67, then, 67 − 21 = ___. 67 − 46 = ___. (b): If 198 − 98 = 100, then, 100 + ___ = 198. 198 − ___ = 98. (c): If 189 + 98 = 287, then, 287 − 98 = ___. 287 − 189 = ___. (d): If 872 − 672 = 200, then, 200 + ___ = 872. 872 − ___ = 672.

Book item: In each of the following, write the subtraction and addition sentences that follow from the given sentence. (a): If 78 + 164 = 242, then, (b): If 462 + 839 = 1,301, then, (c): If 921 − 137 = 784, then, (d): If 824 − 234 = 590, then,
Book item: A minibus has 18 litres of fuel left. After refuelling, the fuel meter indicates 65 litres. How much fuel has been filled in the fuel tank of the minibus?
Book item: What is the difference between 82 and 37? Check your answer. Is 37 + ___ = 82?
Book item: In each of the boxes above, state whether the sums are even or odd. Explain why this is happening.
Book item: What is the difference between two successive sums in each box? Is it the same throughout?
Book item: What will be the difference between two successive sums for (a): 5 consecutive numbers; (b): 6 consecutive numbers?

Book item: Notice how the sums of 3, 4, and 5 consecutive numbers are related to the numbers being added. Use your understanding to find the following sums without adding the numbers directly. (a): 67 + 68 + 69; (b): 24 + 25 + 26 + 27; (c): 48 + 49 + 50 + 51 + 52; (d): 237 + 238 + 239 + 240 + 241 + 242.
Book item: One of the places on the North-South Corridor was 1,855 km from Srinagar and 1,862 km from Kanniyakumari. What was the total length of the North-South Corridor in 2019?

Book item: Mahesh and his family decide to drive from Srinagar to Kanniyakumari. He spends ₹21,880 on fuel and toll tax, and ₹38,900 on other expenses during this journey. How much did he spend in total?

Book item: Find the following sums. Try not to write ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones at the top. Just align the digits properly, at least for the smaller numbers. (a): 238 + 367; (b): 1,234 + 12,345; (c): 12 + 123; (d): 46,120 + 12,890; (e): 878 + 8,789; (f): 1,749 + 17,490.

Book item: The great Indian road trip! Nazrana and her friends planned a road trip across India, starting from Delhi. They first drove to Mumbai, then Goa, then Hyderabad, and finally Puri. Look at the distances marked on the map and help them find the total distance travelled.
Book item: Find 2 numbers among 5,205, 6,220, 7,095, 8,455, and 4,840 whose sum is closest to the following. (a): 10,000; (b): 15,000; (c): 13,000; (d): 16,000.

Book item: The total distance of the sea route from Mumbai to Chennai is 2,700 km. A ship starting from Mumbai first reaches the Cochin port, travelling 1,083 km by sea. How much more distance does it have to travel to reach the Chennai port?

Book item: As you learnt earlier, the longest land route is 15,150 km between Talon (Russia) and Sagres (Portugal). The longest highway in Africa is 10,228 km long, connecting the cities of Cairo, in Egypt and Cape Town, in South Africa. How much longer is the land route between Talon and Sagres compared to the highway between Cairo and Cape Town?

Book item: Subtract the following. Try not to write ten thousands, thousands, hundreds, tens and ones at the top. Align the digits carefully. (a): 4,578 − 2,222; (b): 15,324 − 11,780; (c): 5,423 − 423; (d): 123 − 12; (e): 77,777 − 777; (f): 826 − 752.

Book item: Mary's train journey to Delhi. Mary is on a train journey. She starts from Kolkata with ₹12,540. She spends ₹3,275 on food and other expenses during her trip to Varanasi. In Varanasi, her uncle gives her a gift worth ₹4,900. She then travels to Delhi, spending ₹2,645 on the train ticket. She spends ₹1,275 on souvenirs in Delhi. How much money is Mary left with at the end of the Delhi trip?

Book item: Members of a school council have raised ₹70,500. They plan to setup a Maths Lab with some games and models worth ₹39,785, buy library books worth ₹9,545, and purchase sports equipment worth ₹19,548. (a): Estimate whether the school council has raised enough money to make the purchases. Share your thoughts in the class. (b): Check your estimate with calculations.

Book item: A truck can carry 8,250 kg of goods. A factory loads 3,675 kg of cement and 2,850 kg of steel on it. (a): What is the total weight loaded onto the truck? (b): How much more weight can the truck carry before reaching its maximum capacity?

Book item: Ambrish saved ₹92,375 over a year to buy cows and goats. He buys a cow for ₹26,000 and a goat for ₹17,000. He also buys a milking machine for ₹19,873. Does he have enough money to buy these? How much more or less does he have than he needs?
Book item: A factory produces 54,000 nuts and bolts in a day. An order is placed for 85,300 nuts and bolts. How many more nuts and bolts does the factory need to produce to complete the order?
Book item: Virat Kohli has scored 27,599 runs. He has 6,758 runs less than Sachin Tendulkar. How many runs has Sachin Tendulkar scored?

Book item: Sukanta likes the numbers 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000. He wants to figure out what number he should add to a given number such that the sum is 100 or 1,000. Help him fill in the blank with an appropriate number. 32 + ___ = 100
Book item: Try this method for the number 59. 59 + ___ = 100
Book item: Now, use this method to solve the following. 877 + ___ = 1,000 and 666 + ___ = 1,000; 4,103 + ___ = 10,000 and 5,555 + ___ = 10,000.

Book item: Will this method work if the units digit is 0? What do you think? What other methods can you use to find the missing number to fill in the blanks? Share your thoughts in the class. (a): 180 + ___ = 1,000; (b): 760 + ___ = 1,000; (c): 400 + ___ = 1,000.

Book item: Namita likes the number 9. She wants to subtract 9 or 99 from any number. Find a way to quickly subtract 9 or 99 from any number. (a): 67 − 9 = ___; (b): 83 − 9 = ___; (c): 144 − 9 = ___; (d): 187 − 99 = ___; (e): 247 − 99 = ___; (f): 763 − 99 = ___.

Book item: Now, use the above solutions to find answers to the following problems. Do not calculate again. Namita wonders if she can get 9 or 99 as the answer to any subtraction problem. Find a way to get the desired answer. (a): 32 − ___ = 9; (b): 56 − ___ = 9; (c): 877 − ___ = 99; (d): 666 − ___ = 99.

Book item: Nitin likes numbers that read the same when read from left to right or from right to left. Such numbers are called palindrome numbers. The numbers 22, 363, 404, and 8,558 are some examples. List all palindrome numbers between 100 and 200.
Book item: List all palindrome numbers between 900 and 1,200.
Book item: List all palindrome numbers between 25,000 and 27,000.
Book item: In a 3×3 grid, arrange the numbers 1 to 9 such that each row and each column has numbers in an increasing (inc) order. Each number should be used only once.
Book item: This time, fill the grid such that each row and column has numbers in decreasing (dec) order.

Book item: Now, fill the grids below with numbers (1 to 9) based on the inc (increasing) and dec (decreasing) conditions, as indicated below. Grid 1: the rows are dec, dec, dec and the columns are inc, inc, inc.
Book item: Fill the grid with numbers 1 to 9 as indicated. Grid 2: the rows are dec, dec, inc and the columns are dec, dec, inc.
Book item: Fill the grid with numbers 1 to 9 as indicated. Grid 3: the rows are inc, inc, dec and the columns are inc, dec, dec.
Book item: Observe the given arrangement. Paired arrangement for 18. Add 2 to 18. What changes or does not change in the arrangement?
Book item: Observe the given arrangement. Paired arrangement for 23. Add 2 to 23. What changes or does not change in the arrangement?

Book item: What do you notice about the sums in each of the following cases? Do you think it will be true for all pairs of such numbers? Explain your observations. You may use the paired arrangement to explain your thinking. (a): 12 and 6 are a pair of even numbers. Choose 5 such pairs of even numbers. Add the numbers in each of the pairs.

Book item: What do you notice about the sums in each of the following cases? Do you think it will be true for all pairs of such numbers? Explain your observations. You may use the paired arrangement to explain your thinking. (b): 13 and 9 are a pair of odd numbers. Choose 5 such pairs of odd numbers. Add the numbers in each of the pairs.

Book item: What do you notice about the sums in each of the following cases? Do you think it will be true for all pairs of such numbers? Explain your observations. You may use the paired arrangement to explain your thinking. (c): 7 and 12 are a pair of odd and even numbers. Choose 5 such pairs of odd and even numbers. Add the numbers in each of the pairs.

Book item: Jincy opened her piggy bank. She found 8 coins of ₹1, 9 coins of ₹2 and 5 coins of ₹5. She wants to buy stickers worth ₹38. What possible combination of coins can she use to pay the exact amount?

Book item: Raghu is fond of his grandfather's torch. He starts playing with it. He presses the switch once and the light turns ON. He presses it a second time and the light turns OFF. He presses the switch a third time and the light turns ON. He keeps doing this several times. Will the torch be ON or OFF after the 23rd press? How do you know?
Book item: For what number of presses will the torch be ON? For what number of presses of the switch will the torch be OFF?

Book item: Priyanka Mohite is the first Indian woman to climb five Himalayan peaks above 8,000 metres. Read the table and answer the questions that follow. (a): Which is the highest peak she climbed? (b): What is the difference in height between the highest and lowest peaks she has climbed, as per the table? (c): What is the difference between heights of Mount Elbrus and Mount Kanchenjunga? (d): If Priyanka was 20 years old when she summited Mount Everest in 2013, in which year was she born?

Book item: For each district, find out if the number of certificates were sufficient? If insufficient, calculate how many certificates fell short. If extra, calculate how many certificates were in excess.
